graduation_requirements.raw_text:
After a student has completed their required 3 math credits, additional math courses will count as technology or elective credits.
The three-year science requirement is designed to expose students to Earth Science, Life Science, and Physical Science subjects.
After a student has completed their required 3 science credits, additional science courses will count as technology or elective credits.
Woodstock sports team participation can be used to satisfy one of the 2 required wellness credits towards graduation. Once a student has reached their 1 credit of sports participation (.25 credits per sports season completed), no additional sports credit will appear on the transcript.
All students are expected to complete the proficiency graduation requirements in Physical Education and Health Education. In order for students to have the opportunity to progress and demonstrate proficiency in the standards prior to graduation, one year of Wellness is required.

courses.description: Algebra is the foundational course for all mathematics. This student led course will have students discussing expressions, equations, inequalities and how to use them to solve problems. Students will be developing modeling skills (creating tables of values, pictures, graphs and equations) to help them make sense of the world around them. The course is structured with small groups discovering mathematical concepts. Students who succeed in this course are ready for Geometry.
courses.prerequisites: Math 8 or Grade 8 Algebra

courses.description: This course is designed to increase students’ problem solving ability. Students will identify patterns and structure, present findings in multiple ways, explain their thinking, critique and debate the findings of their peers, identify errors in reasoning, and reflect on the process of investigation to arrive at a general solution method. Topics include: Geometric structure and notation, an algebra review, the properties and congruence of geometric figures transformations, geometric constructions, coordinate geometry, geometry of circles, and an introduction to trigonometry. Students who succeed in this course are ready for Algebra II.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I

courses.description: Algebra II is designed to further the preparation of students for advanced mathematical study. Students will continue to strengthen their reasoning and problem solving abilities and extend their Algebra I skills through a series of inquiry-based units that cover linear exponential and quadratic functions. Strong emphasis will be based upon deepening our understanding of math by seeking out connections and using productive math discourse.
courses.prerequisites: Geometry

courses.description: This is a college-level algebra course intended to prepare students for Precalculus by reviewing the fundamental concepts of algebra. Topics include equations and inequalities, exponents, radicals, functions, systems of equations, polynomials and applications. College credit may also be awarded through concurrent enrollment in MAT 1230 at VTSU- students will have the opportunity to opt in to the concurrent enrollment class in December/January.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra II

courses.description: This year-long course prepares students for the AP exam in May, and requires students to complete homework nightly and over school breaks. There is a summer assignment for this course, which is due on the first day of class and will be assessed. AP Precalculus prepares students for other college-level mathematics and science courses. Through regular practice, students build deep mastery of modeling and functions, and they examine scenarios through multiple representations. The course framework delineates content and skills common to college precalculus courses that are foundational for careers in mathematics, physics, biology, health science, social science, and data science. A graphing calculator is required for this course (recommended TI-84).
courses.prerequisites: Algebra II (recommend B or better)

courses.description: This year-long course prepares students for the AP exam in May, and requires students to complete homework nightly and over school breaks. There is a summer assignment for this course, which is due on the first day of class and will be assessed. In this course, students will study (at least) all topics from the College Board’s Calculus AB course description. The course approach combines lecture, large and small group work, projects, individual work, and appropriate use of technology. The course includes a variety of approaches of varying degrees of formality: theory is balanced with concrete examples. Students can expect to learn topics ranging from limits through derivatives, simple differential equations, antiderivatives, and integrals. Polynomial, rational, and transcendental functions are also studied. A graphing calculator, preferably with the capabilities of a TI-84, is required for this course.
courses.prerequisites: Pre-Calculus

courses.description: This course will review all of the topics in the College Board syllabus for Calculus AB and extend the understanding of calculus to additional functions including parametric, polar, and vector functions. Additional techniques of antidifferentiation and improper integrals will be explored. Students will also study Series and Polynomial Approximations. A graphing calculator with the capabilities of a TI-84 is required for this course. The AP Exam, given in May, is a focus for this course.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Calculus AB

courses.description: This year-long course prepares students for the AP exam in May, and requires students to complete homework nightly and over school breaks. There is a summer assignment for this course, which is due on the first day of class and will be assessed. This is a college-level statistics course that introduces students to the major concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing, and drawing conclusions from data. Students cultivate their understanding of statistics using technology, investigations, problem solving, and writing as they explore concepts like variation and distribution; patterns and uncertainty; and data-based predictions, decisions, and conclusions. College credit may also be awarded through concurrent enrollment in MAT 2021 at VTSU- students will have the opportunity to opt in to the concurrent enrollment class in December/January. A graphing calculator is required for the class (TI84 is recommended).
courses.prerequisites: Algebra II is required (recommend B or better). PreCalculus or Data Science I is preferred.
courses.notes: This course counts towards the CRAFT credential.

courses.description: In this semester-long course, Computer Assisted Design (CAD), students will learn to understand and use representation systems to solve geometric problems in space and in three-dimensional figures drawn in the plane. Students will mainly work with Geogebra, Geoenzo, SketchUp, AutoCAD, GIMP and Sweet home 3D integrating their knowledge of geometry within technological processes and in everyday life applications. Students will be creating their own designs based on different strategies and mathematical definitions. They will learn by developing their computer and drafting skills; describing, comparing, and questioning their representations as a tool of communication which are formalized as mathematical models.
courses.prerequisites: Geometry

courses.description: This course will introduce students to the main ideas in data science through tools such as Google Sheets, Data Commons and Tableau. Students will learn to be data explorers in project-based units, through which they will develop their understanding of data analysis, sampling, correlation/causation, data ethics, modeling with data, algorithmic thinking and basics of programming. This course provides a skill set useful in AP Statistics and AP Computer Science.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra II or concurrent enrollment in Algebra II
courses.notes: This course counts towards the CRAFT credential.

courses.description: A continuation of Data Science I, this course furthers the study of data with an understanding of probability, data collection and cleaning, predictive modeling and machine learning, making and evaluating data-based arguments, and the power of data in society. At the end of the course students will have a portfolio of their data science work to showcase their newly developed abilities. This course provides a skill set useful in AP Statistics and AP Computer Science.
courses.prerequisites: Data Science I
courses.notes: This course counts towards the CRAFT credential.

courses.description: This course will prepare students to be competent consumers in today’s world. The instructional approach combines lecture, large and small group work, projects, individual work, and appropriate use of technology. Personal Finance includes topics that will be of practical use beyond the classroom such as budgeting, taxes, and banking. Students who succeed in this course will be prepared mathematically for life after high school.

This course teaches the programming skills needed to design and publish games online. Students learn fundamental computing skills while designing, coding, and debugging their own computer games. Students will work on basic math, geometry, physical outputs using our laser cutter or 3D-printer, and visual design. Game designer John Romero says that “programming is a creative art form based in logic”, and this class aims to help students experience this from many angles. Communication and collaboration are emphasized. Students are encouraged to take this Game Design course in the same year as Computer Programming: Robotics, which together will provide the background to ensure a smooth transition into AP and college-level computer science courses. Also available for ½ technology credit.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I

courses.description: This course teaches programming skills in the context of robotics. Students start by building small vehicles that are fully controlled by humans. As the vehicles face more complex challenges, the students learn foundational programming concepts to automate and improve the vehicle's handling. Experimentation and collaboration are emphasized. Students test and refine standard algorithms while also looking through a citizenship lens at the impacts of robots and automation in society. Students are encouraged to take this Robotics course in the same year as Computer Programming: Game Design, which together will provide the background to ensure a smooth transition into AP and college-level computer science courses. Also available for ½ technology credit.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I

courses.description: This course covers the curriculum described in the College Board’s Advanced Placement Course Description for Computer Science, which is roughly equivalent to a 1st semester college course in computer science. The course approach combines projects, programming exercises, independent study, and group work. Students use the Java programming language to learn important programming structures, algorithms, and the principles of object-oriented programming. They experience multiple programming tools used by professionals and contribute to a real-world software project used by people outside the classroom. The Advanced Placement exam, given in May, is a course focus and requirement.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I

courses.description: AP Computer Science Principles offers a multidisciplinary approach to teaching the underlying principles of computation. The course introduces students to the creative aspects of programming, abstractions, algorithms, large data sets, the Internet, cybersecurity concerns. In addition to deepening their skills as programmers, students think creatively and apply rigorous analysis techniques to current societal issues in computing. The Advanced Placement exam — which is composed of one in-class project and a traditional multiple-choice exam — is a course focus and requirement.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I

courses.description: Self-driving cars, Google Translate, photo apps that recognize your face, voice assistants like Siri and Alexa, these are all systems built on the principles of Artificial Intelligence (AI). This one-semester course is an introduction to the algorithms used by programmers for teaching computers how to make decisions in uncertain environments. While the field of AI is rigorous and highly practical, it is also a field that is rich with puzzles and games. As such our readings, assignments, and structured projects will be focused on playful AI systems. Prior to taking this class, students must have already gained a strong foundation in programming. This class is largely self-paced and students must be comfortable troubleshooting independently while programming alone and in small groups which is why there is a programming prerequisite.
courses.prerequisites: One semester or another Computer Programming / Computer Science class

courses.description: Students start this one-semester course by taking a deeper look at a few specific fields in the domain of Artificial Intelligence, including risks and benefits to society. The students then research, design, and implement their own AI system using data from a topic that interests them. Students in this class are expected to work largely independently, doing most of their programming outside of class, with class sessions generally being seminar-style discussions of AI issues and programming problems.
courses.prerequisites: Artificial Intelligence I

courses.description: Integrated Environmental Science (IES) offers all 9th grade students an introduction to the core subjects of biology, physics, chemistry and earth systems through the examination of major, relevant themes in science. The course approach combines questioning, experimentation, observation, data analysis, small and large group work, and projects. The goal of this course is to build in each student a foundation in the core subjects, while developing the laboratory, critical thinking, problem solving, technology and communication skills necessary to be an engaged citizen scientist in the 21st century.
courses.notes: This course counts towards the CRAFT credential.

courses.description: Students will engage with the ideas of the Periodic Table and Atomic Theory, Chemical Bonds, Chemical Reactions, Stoichiometry (mathematical applications of Chemistry), begin their thinking about Acids & Bases and Thermochemistry, and employ their Algebra I skills on a regular basis. Students will be expected to participate in a wide variety of science practices including, but not limited to: computational thinking, modeling, and investigating. This course features significant lab work and is a prerequisite for the AP Chemistry course. *May be taken concurrently with IES.
courses.prerequisites: IES*, Algebra I

courses.description: Students will engage with a variety of ideas in Physics including, but not limited to: Kinematics (the study of motion), Forces, Collisions, Sound and Thermodynamics. Students will be expected to participate in a wide variety of science practices such as Analyzing, Explaining, Modeling, and Communicating. Students will employ their Algebra I skills on a regular basis. This course features significant lab work. *May be taken concurrently with IES.
courses.prerequisites: IES*, Algebra I

courses.description: Students taking Biology will focus their learning on four major topics: cell structures, matter and energy, inheritance and genetics, and evolution and natural selection. The course approach combines questioning, modeling, discussion, experimentation, observation, data analysis, and small and large group work. The goal of this course is to build in each student a foundation for biology, while developing the science and engineering practices necessary for argumentation and critical thinking in the real world.This course features significant lab work and is a prerequisite course for AP Biology. *May be taken concurrently with IES.
courses.prerequisites: IES*

courses.description: The AP Biology course is designed to be the equivalent of the general biology course usually taken during the first college year. In Advanced Placement Biology, students will cultivate their understanding of biology through inquiry-based investigations as they explore the following topics: biochemistry, cellular energy, cell signaling, genetics, inheritance and evolution. This course is very molecular and cellular focused. Students will build critical thinking and observation skills, laboratory and presentation techniques, and studying / test taking skills This course features significant lab work.
courses.prerequisites: IES, Biology, Recommendation: Chemistry

courses.description: The AP Chemistry course is designed to be the equivalent of the general chemistry course usually taken during the first college year. This AP course addresses the areas of Periodic Table trends, Bonding and Energy, Stoichiometry, Chemical Equilibrium, Rates and Energetics of reactions, and more. With this curriculum framework as its foundation, students who take the AP Chemistry course will also develop advanced inquiry and reasoning skills such as designing a plan for collecting data, analyzing data, applying mathematical routines, and connecting concepts in and across domains. The result will be readiness for the study of advanced topics in subsequent college courses.
courses.prerequisites: IES, Chemistry, Algebra II

courses.description: In AP Physics 1, students will develop advanced inquiry and reasoning skills to understand objects in motion, forces that account for those motions, and the underlying laws of nature. The structure of the class combines fun and engaging student-led investigations, which invite students to collect and analyze data, with opportunities to apply mathematical routines on problem sets and test practice in order to connect concepts in and across domains. Areas of study include Motion (Kinematics), Forces (Dynamics), Work, Energy, Power, Torque and Momentum for both linear and rotational systems. Additional topics include Oscillations and Fluids. The course is designed to be the equivalent of the introductory Physics course usually taken during the first college year (often referred to as “Mechanics”), and is recommended for students with a solid foundation in Algebra I and Geometry.
courses.prerequisites: IES, Geometry

courses.description: Have you ever wondered how the interactions of microscopic particles cause observable phenomena like static electricity, thermodynamic processes, nuclear reactions, and atomic emission lines? In AP Physics 2: Algebra-Based, you’ll learn about thermodynamics, electricity and magnetics, and quantum, atomic, and nuclear physics. While learning about the key course concepts, you’ll do hands-on laboratory work to investigate specific phenomena. It is designed to be the equivalent of a second-semester introductory college course in algebra-based physics.
courses.prerequisites: Physics OR AP Physics 1, and Geometry.

courses.description: In Advanced Placement Environmental Science, students will observe and critically analyze environmental problems in order to understand the relationships between natural systems on Earth. Major units covered are the living world, populations, air pollution, aquatic and terrestrial pollution, energy and climate change, and land use. The structure of this class will combine laboratory work, case studies, readings, test practice and field trips to cover topics included in the Environmental Science AP Examination. Students will build critical thinking and observation skills, laboratory and presentation techniques and studying/test taking skills.
courses.prerequisites: IES
courses.notes: This course counts towards the CRAFT credential.

courses.description: In this introductory design course, students will develop both “hard skills” (2- and 3-D drawing programs, coding with Arduinos, machine work, tools work, etc.) and “soft skills” (ideation, empathy, collaboration, etc.) with an emphasis on short, challenging, and common projects (that is, all students or student teams working on similar projects at any given moment). A main goal of this course is to develop students who can identify “needs” of others and develop solutions to meet those needs via an appropriate technology choice. Successful completion of this course is necessary for students to enroll in the Innovation Studio course.
courses.notes: This course counts towards the CRAFT credential.

courses.description: In this course, students will focus on the study of the natural world including topics such as the cycles of the sky, the solar system, the role of gravity, and astronomical history. Students will work in cooperative groups, perform lab experiments with simulation software, and complete a variety of classroom assignments. Students can expect to develop their observational abilities, reading and writing skills, and mathematical abilities. It is expected that students will complete science projects and study scientific principles through this particular discipline.

In this course, students will engage in a collaborative, modular furniture installation for the studio and an independent, largely self-directed project. The independent projects should have a clearly defined individual or community need and be able to develop workable solutions. Though largely self-directed, students will be overseen by an instructor and will have regular meetings to share and discuss goals and progress, identify essential next steps, and communicate their work to the outside world. Providing and receiving critique from classmates and instructors will be an important part of this course. *This course counts towards the CRAFT credential. REGENERATIVE AGRICULTURE *Spring (previously named Foundations of Agriculture ) Grades 9, 10, 11,12 ½ credit Foundational Course CRAFT Credential: Take prior to Sustainable Food Systems Elective Eating is an agricultural act and one we participate in every day in order to sustain ourselves. In Regenerative Agriculture, students will work in a hands-on capacity both indoors and out to gain knowledge about how to grow their own food by using regenerative practices such as assessing and building soil health, no-till, cover cropping, organic pest management and biodiversity. Students will learn about starting plants from seed and transplanting practices from our greenhouse to our garden. Students will be planting, harvesting, preparing and eating food grown in our school garden. Students will be responsible for growing, harvesting, and processing microgreens for our staff CSA. Students will be involved with maple sugaring production at the King Farm. Students will get to learn about and visit local farms using these practices as well as plan their own biologically diverse garden model. *This course counts towards the CRAFT credential. SUSTAINABLE FOOD SYSTEMS *Fall (previously named Food and Forest Systems) Grades 9, 10, 11,12 ½ credit Foundational Course CRAFT Credential: Take after Regenerative Agriculture Elective The way our food is grown, processed, transported and distributed is part of a complex system that depends on social, economic and environmental factors. In this course, students will apply a systems thinking lens to understand their place in the food system and find leverage points for making sustainable changes. Students will participate in native plant production, seed saving, and composting as part of a thriving local food system model. Students will be responsible for growing, harvesting and distributing our staff microgreen CSA. Students will get to harvest, prepare and eat locally grown food while tracing the path various foods take to get to their plate. Students will visit local producers to see the process of making various VT products.
courses.prerequisites: Skill-building for Innovation or permission from instructor.
courses.notes: This course counts towards the CRAFT credential.

courses.description: The study of Marine Biology and Oceanography utilizes many different science disciplines to explore a variety of marine ecosystems, including coral reefs, rocky intertidal zones, salt marshes, mangroves, as well as open ocean and deep ocean communities. The first part of the course will focus on an overview of the oceans, the topography of the ocean floor, ocean chemistry, and currents. The second part will focus on major organisms occupying specific habitats throughout diverse marine environments. The third and final major topic covered will be human interactions and environmentally relevant issues such as climate change, aquaculture, and the use of our natural resources.

Modern World History is a one-year, one-credit course that focuses on the historical and cultural development of the modern world. The beginning of the year will focus on the political, cultural, and economic transformations that occurred as a result of global exploration. Following global exploration, students will examine the various political and economic revolutions that reshaped various societies and the world as a whole. Similarly, students will have the opportunity to delve into the major political, social, and economic factors that gave rise to the global conflicts of the first half of the 20th century. Finally, students will explore emerging social, political and economic trends surrounding globalization, and connect these back to earlier units of study. By the end of the course students will demonstrate a greater understanding of the modern world and its historical legacy.

This course follows a thematic and chronological approach in order for students to learn about the cultural, social, political, and economic history of the United States. Within the unit of study students will explore the specific events that defined the eras in United States history while simultaneously recognizing how many issues confronting Americans transcend time. The instructional approach will be through group work and discussion, lecture, and research as students move into the realm of complex synthesis, analysis and evaluation of the cultural, political and economic history of the United States. Students will employ skills such as the investigation and analysis of documents, essay writing, debating, in-class discussion, and peer collaboration.
courses.prerequisites: Modern World

courses.description: This is a rigorous, college-level survey course in preparation for the AP exam and requires a great deal of student commitment. Students should come to this course with strong writing, reading comprehension, and analytical skills. This course requires students to be fully prepared to participate in discussions, activities and document analysis. In preparation for the AP exam students will learn to compose lengthy essays in a limited time while using their historical understanding to meet the demands of multiple types of questions. In class, students will also have the opportunity to participate in simulations, structured debates, and micro-research projects.
courses.prerequisites: Modern World

courses.description: Through the introduction of content and the practice of skills, this year-long course examines the foundations of American government; the structure and principles of the Constitution; checks and balances among the three branches; the bureaucracy; the rights and freedoms provided to citizens; the role of the citizen, interest groups, political parties, the mass media in shaping government policy; and the development of domestic and foreign policies. This course is taught with the understanding that the American democratic system of government requires an informed citizenry that actively engages in the political process. Special attention is given to viewing issues through different perspectives.
courses.prerequisites: US History

courses.description: This year-long course prepares students for the AP exam in May, and requires students to complete homework nightly and over school breaks. Through the introduction of content and the practice of skills, the class examines the foundations of American government; the structure and principles of the Constitution; checks and balances among the three branches; the bureaucracy; the rights and freedoms provided to citizens; the role of the citizen, interest groups, political parties, the mass media in shaping government policy; and the development of domestic and foreign policies. This course is taught with the understanding that the American democratic system of government requires an informed citizenry that actively engages in the political process. Special attention is given to viewing issues through different perspectives.
courses.prerequisites: US History or AP US History

courses.description: Embark on an unforgettable journey through time and cultures in AP Art History! This college-level course explores the stories behind 250 incredible works of art from prehistoric times to the present, representing diverse artistic traditions from around the globe. As an AP Art History student, you’ll become an active participant in the global art world. You’ll investigate how art is created, interpreted, and experienced across different cultures. Through dynamic discussions, creative projects, and in-depth research, you’ll uncover the fascinating connections between history, society, and artistic expression. Get ready to think critically, express your ideas, and explore the power of art in shaping our world. If you’re curious about history, culture, and creativity, AP Art History is your opportunity to see the world in a whole new way!
courses.fulfills_text: This may be used for an Art or Social Studies (elective) credit
courses.notes: Also listed in Visual Arts (Level I, p.43); catalog says it may be used for an Art or Social Studies (elective) credit

courses.description: “Understanding Environmental Issues Through An Economic Lens” Economics is really all about decision making. When looking at environmental issues we have hard choices to make. This course will allow students to examine ways in which economic decision making can have an impact on the environment. Through a variety of simulations, inquiries and real world learning, students will explore environmental issues through an economic lens.
courses.prerequisites: Modern World
courses.notes: This course counts towards the CRAFT credential.

courses.description: Life is social whenever we interact with others. Do we shape society, or does society shape us? How does social change happen? In this course we will explore human interaction through a sociological lens focusing on current research. We will examine social structures like race, gender, and social class; social institutions; shared beliefs of a common culture; and deviance. Student interests guide individual choice projects and class discussions.
courses.prerequisites: Modern World

courses.description: Where is the line between normal and abnormal? Is there really such a thing as free will? This semester-long course is designed for students who would like a better understanding of the many factors that motivate human behavior. We focus on current research with a positive emphasis on mental health and brain physiology. Specific topics include personality, gender, ethics, altered states of consciousness, abnormal behavior, social dynamics. Student interests guide individual choice projects and class discussions.
courses.prerequisites: Modern World

courses.description: Philosophy nurtures complex thinking by asking students to investigate enduring questions, such as: What does it mean to be good? Should we have laws that protect individuals from themselves? Is it moral to tell a white lie? Students in the course consider these questions as they study groundbreaking philosophers and share their own theories in class discussions, debates, and writings. Many of the videos and readings in the course are inspired by the class “Justice,” taught by Harvard University political philosopher Michael Sandel.
courses.prerequisites: AP U.S. Government & Politics or U.S. Government & Politics

courses.description: This course will examine the role that ideas about race played in shaping the culture, government, and economy of the United States—and the extent to which discriminatory policies of the past continue to impact the lives of Americans. We'll consider the question: To what extent does race still matter in America? And how does Vermont fit into the equation? Finally, we'll look at how we might most effectively promote the cause of racial justice today. This course will delve into controversial and sensitive topics. Students will need to be willing to share their opinions and to remain open to others' perspectives.
courses.prerequisites: U.S. History or AP U.S. History

courses.description: This course will explore current events from a global perspective. Possible topics of study include politics, government, war, poverty, genocide, racism, the environment, minorities, and human rights. Central questions to contemplate would be: What are the world’s most pressing issues? What are possible solutions? What is the role of the US nationally and internationally in the 21st century? And, what is the role of the individual on the local, state, national and global levels? Throughout the semester, students will be involved in a variety of activities including research papers, oral presentations, writing and reading assignments.
courses.prerequisites: Modern World

courses.description: In this course, students will explore how literary and informational texts help us understand our identities and the perspectives of others. Students will investigate perplexing questions, such as, can there ever be a perfect society? How do stories help people make sense of the world? How can art serve as a vehicle for social change? And how can literature help me understand the points of view of others? They will share their voices and perspectives through a variety of writing and speaking opportunities, including reflective and informative essays, creative writing assignments, argumentative writing assignments, Socratic discussions, and informative presentations. Students will work towards proficiency on the 9/10 Common Core English Language Arts Standards in reading, writing, language, and speaking and listening.
courses.notes: Reading/Writing Level: All abilities

courses.description: In English 10, students will study selected works of American authors in order to investigate, interpret, and question the concepts of the American Dream and our American identity. By studying a variety of genres, students will sharpen their critical reading skills as they continue to develop their voice, style, and purpose as writers. Students will continue to develop annotation strategies, as well as discussion techniques. Journaling, analytical essay writing, vocabulary development, reinforcement of Standard English conventions, along with attention to diction and syntax are all skills and practices tenth grade students will engage over their course of study in English II. Students will be expected to reach proficiency or beyond on the 9/10 Common Core English Language Arts Standards in reading, writing, language, and speaking and listening.
courses.prerequisites: English I
courses.notes: Reading/Writing Level: All abilities

courses.description: In English III, students read a variety of texts, including memoirs, novellas, novels, graphic novels, short stories, informational texts, and literary classics. Students use these texts as a way to explore a range of topics and themes of real-world importance and relevance, and they explore those texts through discussions and both formal and informal writing. Students practice reading, writing, and critical thinking skills, and they engage in meaningful conversations as we learn about and practice civil discourse. They learn about the art of persuasion and how to use rhetorical devices to make compelling arguments. Vocabulary, research, and grammar will continue as integrated focus points in the curriculum throughout the year. Students will be expected to reach proficiency on the 11/12 Common Core English Language Arts Standards in: reading, writing, language, and speaking and listening.
courses.prerequisites: English I and II
courses.notes: Reading/Writing Level: All abilities

courses.description: In English IV, we will study literary fiction and non-fiction and learn some essential media literacy skills. Students will build on their writing skills from previous years, beginning with email writing and the personal narrative or college application essay and continuing with analytical writing in response to texts. Additionally, we will spend considerable time developing speaking and listening skills so that students feel prepared to engage in productive, civil discourse about a range of “real-world” topics. Students will be expected to reach proficiency on the 11/12 Common Core English Language Arts Standards in: reading, writing, language, and speaking and listening.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of English I, II, III

courses.description: AP English Language and Composition is an introductory college-level composition course that focuses on rhetorical analysis and argumentation. Students engage in meaningful discussions and address questions of real-world importance as they practice and apply college-ready reading and writing skills. They read rigorous texts from various eras and in different genres, analyzing the big ideas of rhetorical situations, claims/evidence, reasoning/organization, and style.They research topics of particular interest to them, practice evidence-based analytic and argumentative writing, and learn how authors make choices to communicate with their audience. In addition to preparing students for college, this course will help them enter into conversations that should empower them to participate in your community as responsible citizens. In addition, students are provided with AP test materials so that they can prepare for the AP exam. Students are expected to complete the summer reading assignment by mid-August and to take the AP English Language and Composition Exam in May.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of English I, II
courses.notes: Mandatory Summer Reading and Writing Assignment; Reading/Writing Level: Advanced

courses.description: AP English Literature and Composition is an introductory college level literature course where students gain practice, experience and expertise in close reading and analysis of literature (short stories, novels, poetry, drama). While students do spend some time working on personal narratives (college essays) in the early fall, literary analysis, both oral and in writing,is their focus for much of the course, which emphasizes literature-to-life connections. Students are expected to complete the summer reading assignment by early August and to take the national AP Literature and Composition Exam in May.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of English I, II
courses.notes: Mandatory Summer Reading and Writing Assignment; Reading/Writing Level: Advanced

courses.description: This semester-long course provides the opportunity for students to learn the fundamentals of journalism through planning, writing, editing, and photography. We will also explore the First Amendment and the media’s role in relation to this freedom. A primary emphasis will be placed on journalistic writing in a variety of different styles including: news stories, features, reviews, and editorials. Grammar, usage, and mechanics’ skills will be taught and reinforced in the editing process.
courses.fulfills_text: Elective. Note: This course is worth ½ an elective credit for 9th-11th graders. Seniors have the possibility of earning ½ English credit for this course, with prior approval from a school counselor.

courses.description: Literacy Study is a targeted literacy support class designed to help students develop their reading skills, and to support them in their current standards-aligned classwork. We utilize the Rewards Curriculum, a research validated program to improve students’ reading fluency, comprehension, and vocabulary knowledge. In addition, students will work on pre-existing classwork from English class or any other class featuring literacy skills, with support and encouragement from their Literacy Study teacher. This course is available at different levels depending on student needs. Level I uses the Rewards Secondary curriculum, and Level II uses the Rewards Social Studies curriculum. Students are referred to this class based on teacher, parent, or counselor input, and are screened for eligibility before placement.

Advanced Literacy Study is a targeted literacy support class designed to help students develop their reading skills, and to support them in their current standards-aligned classwork. We utilize the Rewards Curriculum, a research validated program to improve students’ reading fluency, comprehension, and vocabulary knowledge. In addition, students will work on pre-existing classwork from English class or any other class featuring literacy skills, with support and encouragement from their Literacy Study teacher. Advanced Literacy Study builds upon previous instruction in Literacy Study, and uses the Science curriculum of the Rewards program. Students are referred to this class based on teacher, parent, or counselor input, and are screened for eligibility before placement.

Welcome to Supported Study, a targeted executive functioning support class designed to help students succeed in their current standards-aligned coursework. Executive functioning refers to the mental skills needed to manage tasks effectively, including planning, organizing, and staying focused. In this class, students will learn to set achievable goals, develop strong organizational habits, and practice self-reflection to monitor their progress. Through personalized strategies, students build the tools necessary to improve time management, complete assignments on time, and excel in their academic work. Students are referred to this class based on teacher, parent, or counselor input.
courses.credits_text: ½ general elective credit per semester

courses.description: French I is an introduction to French language and culture. This course will give students the ability to discuss themselves, family, friends, school, and daily life. The course is conducted primarily in French and students are expected to speak and write French creatively in this novice language course to practice what we are learning. The study of French culture is an integral part of each lesson. The curriculum is highly interactive and tied to student interest. Thematic content is drawn from current events and authentic resources. Students will engage in fun and stimulating games, dialogues, skits, projects, videos, and music selections from authentic resources.

Students continue to develop their ability to speak, understand, read and write French. The class is conducted primarily in French, oral work is emphasized, and self-initiated conversation is encouraged. Students continue learning vocabulary and will be able to converse and write using present, past, and future tenses. The study of French culture is an integral part of each lesson. The curriculum is highly interactive and tied to student interest. Thematic content is drawn from current events and authentic resources. Students will engage in fun and stimulating games, dialogues, skits, projects, videos, and music selections from authentic resources.

Students continue to develop their ability to speak, understand, read and write French. The course is taught primarily in French. Each unit of study includes grammar, verb, and vocabulary acquisition which are applied in assignments. Students are introduced to literature. Cultural studies include art, music, history, and the French speaking areas of the world. The curriculum is highly interactive and tied to student interest. Thematic content is drawn from current events and authentic resources. Students will engage in interesting dialogues, skits, projects, videos, and music selections from authentic resources.

This course is conducted in French and students will make use of both literary and cultural texts as well as the Internet to strengthen their French speaking and writing abilities, and to deepen their understanding of French culture and civilization. Students will review previously studied grammar and will be required to write on contemporary issues. Students will learn about French history through art, architecture, geography, literature and poetry. They will also learn important points that lead to the French RevolutionSuccessful students of French IV can look forward to continuing their studies in either AP French or Advanced Studies in French. Text: Trésors du temps.

This course is an optional preparatory year for the AP test and/or a continuation of deepening students’ fluency in French, French culture—art, literature, geography, values, diversity and current events, and understanding other Francophone cultures. This course is taught in French and students are expected to speak in French during the whole class. Each quarter will focus on a different theme—Global Challenges, Beauty and Art, Contemporary Life, Personal and Public Identities, Families and Communities and Poetry and Literature. Students can expect to expand their speaking skills, along with gaining knowledge of how to express themselves in French for authentic audiences. Additionally, students are expected to use authentic audios and videos to perfect their speaking and listening skills. They will also be required to work independently on at least two presentations projects and present them to the class and invited guests. If they choose to take the Advanced Placement, the exam will be in May. E-texts: AP French, Richard Ladd; Allons au-dela and Texts: Une Fois Pour Toutes; Breaking the Barrier

Throughout the year students will study Roman daily life (homes, gladiators, baths, mythology) in the city of Pompeii through readings, supplementary materials, projects, and games. This course introduces students to the ancient Romans through their language, which is the basis of the modern Romance languages. It emphasizes the close relationship of Latin to the understanding of English grammar and vocabulary. The primary text students will use is the first book of the Cambridge Latin Course. Reading comprehension, translation skills, making connections to other languages, learning Latin sayings from ancient authors, and learning about the products and perspectives of the ancient Romans are all key aspects of this course. Students will also begin to build conversational Latin skills so they can ask and answer basic questions about themselves and the texts they read, and so that they can retell familiar stories.

Students will pick up where they left off from their study of ancient Pompeii and the Romans who lived there. They will begin the year learning about Roman practices related to education, religion, and politics, and will dig into more detailed information about the eruption of Mt. Vesuvius. Students will learn more details about what the remains in Pompeii and surrounding archaeological sites can tell us about the ancient world. Later in the year they will learn more about the Romans in Britain and ancient Egypt through increasingly complex readings, supplementary materials, and projects. Throughout the course students will be building their vocabulary and reading comprehension skills and will continue to learn Latin sayings from ancient authors. Connections with English and other languages will continue to be stressed through comparisons of vocabulary and grammar. Students will continue to develop their skills in conversational Latin so they can ask and answer questions about themselves and the progressively more complex texts they read, and so they can retell stories in different tenses. The primary texts will be the first and second books of the Cambridge Latin Course.

Students will continue their study of Roman life and the Roman military in Britain, and will then learn more about the ancient cities of Aquae Sulis and Rome through increasingly more complex readings, supplementary materials, and projects. Students will also begin to read short passages from authentic Latin authors, and may finish their study of the main elements of Latin grammar. Depending on student interest, additional Latin novellas that tell various stories from Roman history and mythology may be read and discussed as a class or individually. Connections with English and other languages continue to be stressed through comparisons of vocabulary and grammar. Reading comprehension and translating as well as written composition and conversation are emphasized.

Latin IV students will use their knowledge to develop an appreciation for various Classical authors through readings in Latin and supplementary materials in translation. Students will also continue their study of Roman history, especially focusing on the end of the Roman Republic and beginning of the empire. By the end of the year, students will have experience reading and analyzing extended passages of authentic Latin poetry and prose and will be familiar with Roman political and literary culture of the early imperial period and beyond. Reading comprehension and translating as well as written composition and conversation are emphasized.

In this semester-long course students will be introduced to the ancient Greek alphabet, basic Greek vocabulary and grammar, and Greek history and mythology. Students will learn about the syntax of a complex inflected language, and will be able to read, hear, write, speak, and understand simple sentences and short stories in Greek. Students will also make connections to English vocabulary, and will better understand the development of languages as a whole. Through readings and presentations in English students will also learn much about the history and mythology of the ancient Greeks. Students will also begin to make inferences about what constituted ancient Greek culture, will learn how that culture changed over time, and will explore how that culture still influences the modern world.

This course is a beginning language course that emphasizes speaking, reading, writing and listening comprehension skills for real-world communication.. The course is conducted primarily in Spanish and students are expected to use Spanish in class to practice what we are learning. The curriculum is highly interactive and tied to student interest and thematic content drawn from current events, authentic resources. The curriculum used at this level is formatted using comprehension-based methods of language instruction. This curriculum, from The Comprehensible Classroom, teaches language and culture simultaneously. Games, skits, presentations and music are incorporated in language learning and assessment.

This course continues to develop the four language skills of speaking, understanding, reading and writing in Spanish. The course is conducted primarily in Spanish and students are expected to use the language in class to the best of their ability. Students continue to acquire practical vocabulary through content specific units and will be able to use and understand different verb tenses including the present, several forms of the past tense and commands. The curriculum used at this level is formatted using comprehension-based methods of language instruction. This curriculum, from The Comprehensible Classroom, teaches language and culture simultaneously, allowing Spanish language learners the opportunity to develop cultural understanding at a depth rarely achieved in beginning language courses. Students will expand their reading comprehension using short stories and articles and their speaking skills through spontaneous conversations. Classroom projects; group and individual, are done in each unit and include games, dialogues, videos, and music.

This course builds on speaking, reading, writing and listening comprehension skills for real-world communication learned in beginning Spanish courses. The course is conducted primarily in Spanish and students are expected to communicate with each other and the instructor in Spanish. Language and culture are taught in context with one another. Student interest guides themes that we’ll explore in depth. Authentic resources, literature and current events provide the basis for our curriculum. Literary texts, cartoons, games, skits, presentations and music are incorporated in language learning and assessment.
courses.notes: This course counts towards the CRAFT credential.

courses.description: In this course students will expand their command and knowledge of Spanish and of Hispanic cultures. They will be able to use and understand the subjunctive mood. They will also write several essay papers and read and analyze short literature pieces. Authentic cultural products such as art work, political and satirical cartoons, contemporary music, news programs, websites and advertisements will prompt students to use the language in a variety of advanced ways. The class is conducted in Spanish and students are expected to use Spanish almost exclusively in class.

This course is designed to prepare the advanced Spanish language student for the Advanced Placement exam in Spanish Language and Culture as well as provide an opportunity to practice the language skills of reading, writing, speaking and listening. A curriculum of six themes, Global Challenges, Science and Technology, Contemporary Life, Personal and Public Identities, Families and Communities and Beauty and Aesthetics, integrates language, content and cultures into an interrelated series of lessons and activities that promote the use of language in a variety of contexts. This class builds communication skills at an academic and professional level in Spanish. Only authentic materials are used. In addition, students will demonstrate an understanding of the products, practices and perspectives of Spanish-speaking countries and their cultures. The class is taught in Spanish and students are expected to speak Spanish exclusively in class.

This rigorous advanced level course is for students who wish to continue their exploration of the Spanish language. The class is organized in a seminar structure with an aim to incorporate student interests and place-based learning. Students research, prepare and lead short seminar discussions on cultural, political and social dimensions of the Spanish-speaking World. Advanced grammar structures are explored in depth. The class is conducted entirely in Spanish and students communicate with one another and the instructor in Spanish at all times.

Digital Art and Design combines digital illustration, painting, photography, and graphic design into one creative, hands-on course. Using state-of-the-art tools such as high-performance computers and iPad Pros provided by the school, you’ll learn how professional artists and designers use digital media to communicate ideas, solve creative problems, and create compelling artwork. You’ll explore digital drawing, painting, and illustration techniques while developing your understanding of color, composition, typography, and the elements and principles of design. Projects may include original character and concept art, expressive portraits, imaginative landscapes, posters, advertisements, digital art, photo manipulation, branding, and other designs for both print and digital media. Along the way, you’ll work with professional digital tools, including Adobe Creative Cloud, while experimenting with digital brushes, layers, blending, photo editing, graphics, and text. You’ll learn how artists and designers make purposeful creative choices and develop the technical skills needed to turn an idea into a polished finished product. Whether you love drawing and painting, are interested in graphic design, fashion, marketing, or business, or simply want to explore what is possible with digital art, this course gives you the freedom to experiment, develop your own artistic style, and build real-world creative skills. This course is also available for ½ technology credit.
courses.notes: Not recommended for students enrolling in ski schools

courses.description: Digital Photography explores the art of photography while learning to use digital cameras, lighting techniques, and professional tools like Adobe Photoshop and Lightroom. No experience? No problem! This beginner-friendly course helps you master the basics of art and design while having fun behind the lens. You’ll tackle exciting photo challenges, experiment with lighting, and explore how to use photography for creative storytelling. Plus, you’ll build your very own blog site to showcase your best shots and personal portfolio. Whether you dream of becoming a professional photographer or just want to explore a new creative outlet, Digital Photography is your chance to capture the world from your unique perspective. This course is also available for ½ technology credit.
courses.notes: Not recommended for students enrolling in ski schools

courses.description: Venture into the world of two-dimensional art as you explore a range of media, including ink, pastel, paint, charcoal, and pencil. Dive into foundational principles of design, perspective, shading, color, and composition, while gaining practical experience drawing from life—whether it’s the human figure, still life, or landscapes—or unleashing the full power of your imagination. As you discover your artistic process, you'll unlock the transformative power of planning, proposing, collaborating, and honing your work. Throughout this journey, you'll also build confidence in reflecting on and communicating your creative ideas. This course isn’t just about making art—it’s about finding your unique voice, evolving as an artist, and sharing your personal perspective.

In this dynamic course, art intersects with nature, activism, and sustainability. Eco Art is an interdisciplinary field that challenges us to investigate, question, and expand upon the relationship between people and nature. Eco-artists often engage their community and use art & design to bring positive change. We will use the outdoors as a studio space, a place for observation, inspiration, and a source for materials. A broad range of media and techniques will be explored; possibilities include sculpture, drawing, painting, printmaking, and collage. As they create, students will learn about environmental artists and ways in which art can address topics like climate change, waste reduction, and biodiversity. We will look for opportunities to collaborate with each other, local artists, other classes, and within the broader community.
courses.notes: This course counts towards the CRAFT credential.

courses.description: This course introduces students to the exciting world of painting and provides a solid foundation in both technical skills and artistic expression. Students will experiment with a variety of materials (watercolor, acrylic, tempera etc.) to discover different methods of creating art. Through open-ended explorations students will learn about color mixing, brush handling, mark making, light and shadow, and basic composition. Students can expect self-directed experimentation, and open-ended projects that explore personal themes and meaningful ideas along the way, as they build confidence in their ability to communicate visually.

Pottery fosters an awareness of form and space through working with clay. Basic handbuilding clay techniques will be taught as well as glazing and surface techniques. Students will have the opportunity to explore basic forms on the pottery wheel. Expect to create functional as well as whimsical pieces as you are challenged to think through the expressive potential of clay. This class requires the ability to work independently, imaginatively and a willingness to take creative risks. Basic practices in the maintenance of a safe and functional workplace will be emphasized.

Ready to level up your creative skills? Advanced Digital Photo and Design is the perfect class for students who’ve taken Graphic Design, Digital Illustration, or Digital Photography and want to push their artistic boundaries even further. This class offers tons of flexibility and creative freedom—you can focus on digital photography, digital art, or an exciting mix of both! Whether you’re building a portfolio for AP 2D Art and Design, prepping for art school, or just eager to explore your creative potential, this class is designed to help you shine. You’ll dive into advanced projects that reflect real-world art college portfolio standards while experimenting with new techniques, styles, and creative concepts. From crafting original photo series and digital illustrations to exploring cutting-edge design trends, you’ll have the chance to develop your artistic voice while learning higher-level design and digital art skills. If you’re passionate about art and ready for a fun, challenging creative adventure, this is the course for you!
courses.prerequisites: Two years of level I art or portfolio review
courses.notes: Not recommended for students enrolling in ski schools

courses.description: Pottery II is a continuation of Pottery. Students will continue to develop clay handbuilding, glazing and surface techniques. Students will also have the opportunity to expand their skills on the pottery wheel. The students will make functional as well as whimsical pieces as they think through the potential of clay, learn to trust intuition and tell meaningful stories sculpturally. Students will be asked to work independently, imaginatively and to take creative risks. There will be a focus on innovation, experimentation and craftsmanship. Basic practices in the maintenance of a safe and functional workplace will be expected. Students who have interest, will have the opportunity to explore other sculpture media such as wire, plaster, and assemblage.
courses.prerequisites: Pottery I

courses.description: This course is designed for students eager to deepen their artistic practice, building on the foundations established in previous studio classes. Through a variety of media and techniques across 2D and 3D art—including drawing, painting, collage, mixed media, clay, and printmaking—students will refine their unique expressive voice. Key components of the course include engaging with visiting artists, exploring local studios and museums, and participating in public exhibitions. These experiences enrich the learning process and help students form a deeper connection to the broader art community. This course provides a transformative opportunity to push creative boundaries, sharpen technical skills, and prepare for the next step in your artistic journey.
courses.prerequisites: Two semesters of level I art courses

courses.description: Advanced Art is designed for experienced students eager to explore personal artistic pathways and deepen their artistic literacy within 2D mediums. Whether you're preparing for AP Art, building a professional portfolio, or ready to elevate your practice, this course provides the structure and guidance you need. Centered around portfolio development, the course aligns with the AP Studio Art Drawing Portfolio guidelines. With a strong emphasis on studio production, it cultivates higher-level thinking, a diverse range of technical skills (across various mediums and styles), as well as art criticism, art history, and aesthetics, offering a comprehensive approach to advancing your skills as an artist.
courses.prerequisites: Two years of level I art or portfolio review

courses.description: This course follows the program of study defined by the Advanced Placement College Program of the Educational Testing Service. As the composition of this curriculum changes from year to year, students are advised to review the AP booklet before enrolling. Information can be found at the Advanced Placement College Board site: https://apstudents.collegeboard.org/course-index-page This class may be of assistance in college application planning. It also provides comfort for students continuing with college-level Studio Art classes. Three options are available for AP Art: AP Drawing: Develop drawing skills in materials and processes, such as drawing, painting, collage, mixed media, and printmaking. AP 3D Art & Design Develop 3-D skills in materials and processes, such as sculpture, architectural rendering and models, metalwork, ceramics, glasswork, etc. AP 2D Art & Design (Photography or Graphic Art) Develop your 2-D skills through materials and processes such as graphic design, photography, collage, printmaking, fashion illustration, and others. This course can be taken in two separate years, with students earning credit both times. Each year focuses on a different portfolio, allowing students to explore new ideas, techniques, and themes. This structure is encouraged by AP Central. The course is open to juniors and seniors. Other AP art courses follow a different pathway and are not designed to be taken twice.
courses.prerequisites: Advanced Level Art in a field of study
courses.notes: Offered in three options (AP Drawing, AP 3D Art & Design, AP 2D Art & Design); can be taken in two separate years with credit both times

courses.description: Concert Choir builds on the foundation developed through the elementary and middle school chorus programs, however, prior choir experience is not required. Students collaborate and become part of our musical community through solo & ensemble performances, festivals, concerts, and travel experiences. Some performances outside of the school day are a required part of the curriculum. Students can take this course more than once for credit.

Concert Band builds on the foundation developed through the 4th-8th grade band programs. Students collaborate and become part of our musical community through solo & ensemble performances, festivals, concerts, and travel experiences. Some performances outside of the school day are a required part of the curriculum. Students without instruments can contact the director for information regarding the use of a school-owned instrument. Students can take this course more than once for credit.
courses.prerequisites: Prior band experience or instructor approval. Students who have not been in band before and would like to begin, should contact the instructor.

courses.description: Jazz/Funk Band builds on the foundation developed through the 5th-8th grade band programs. Students collaborate and become part of our musical community through solo & ensemble performances, festivals, concerts, and travel experiences. Some performances outside of the school day are a required part of the curriculum. Students without instruments can contact the director for information regarding the use of a school-owned instrument. Students can take this course more than once for credit. Guitar and keyboard players should connect with the instructor regarding enrollment.
courses.prerequisites: Concurrent enrollment in Symphonic Band or instructor approval.

courses.description: At Woodstock Union High School health and physical education are combined to create an integrated wellness program that, we believe, provides high school students with the tools they need to achieve a healthy balance in their busy lives. All students are expected to complete the proficiency graduation requirements in Physical Education and Health Education. In order for students to have the opportunity to progress and demonstrate proficiency in the standards prior to graduation, one year of Wellness is required.
courses.notes: This course counts towards the CRAFT credential.; Woodstock sports team participation can be used to satisfy one of the 2 required wellness credits towards graduation (.25 credits per sports season; max 1 credit)

courses.description: At Woodstock Union High School health and physical education are combined to create an integrated wellness program that, we believe, provides high school students with the tools they need to achieve a healthy balance in their busy lives. All students are expected to complete the proficiency graduation requirements in Physical Education and Health Education. Units may include Seasonal Team Games, Net Games, Strength Training and/or Kickboxing and Self-Defense.

courses.description: This is a Pass/Fail life skills course that introduces students to the complex decision making skills necessary for the driving environment. The course will integrate thirty hours of classroom instruction with six hours of behind the wheel training as well as six hours of in-car observation. A student-parent involvement program that requires an additional twenty hours of guided practice is a component for successful completion of the course. It is imperative that the classwork be completed on time because it is necessary to have classroom knowledge of the skills that will be practiced in the driving portion. A student may not take the course more than once due to the limited availability of seats every year. If a student does not pass or complete the course, they must seek alternative ways to complete the course at the expense of the family/guardians of the student outside of the school. Click here for more information and frequently asked questions from the Vermont Department of Motor Vehicles. To Sign up for Driver’s Education click here or use the QR code below.
courses.prerequisites: • The Drivers Education student must be at least 15 years of age by the first day of class. • Students must provide proof to a school administrator of a current, valid Vermont Learner’s permit prior to Aug 1st or Dec 1st. • Students must be in good standing with the administration as well as with the local authorities. • Scheduling order is determined by age. • Interested students should review the policy for Driver’s Education in the Student Handbook. • It is recommended that the student have some driving experience prior to the first day of class.
courses.notes: Pass/Fail life skills course

courses.description: This course will be an opportunity for students to put into place permaculture design practices we can use and learn from in our community. Students in this class will help make decisions about different projects we want to have at the king farm and participate in implementing them. Classes will mostly meet at the King Farm as weather permits. Students will spend their time exploring, learning about, and being immersed at the King Farm which will be a future campus and living learning lab.
courses.notes: This course counts towards the CRAFT credential.; Fall semester

courses.description: This semester course is designed for students who have a strong interest in the environment, agriculture, and forests. Students in this course want to take important actions in order to strengthen our community and be stewards of our land. Students will research, propose, and implement an independent action project that makes a difference in our local community. Students will use the NuVu design process to support the development of their action projects. Through brainstorming, sketching, prototyping, and receiving feedback, they will iteratively develop their project. Project ideas should develop an awareness of the ecological and cultural contexts in which their work is taking place.The final project should be implemented or installed by the end of the course. Projects might include: increasing local food access, designing a sustainable landscape, or planting native trees to make a river healthier. Students will be encouraged to think independently and to extend their learning beyond the classroom through connections with community partners to gain practical, hands-on experience in a variety of settings. Themes of climate resilience, equity, and working within a system will be emphasized through community experiences, while the rest of the course, students will be focused on their action projects. All SAP projects will be presented at the end of the course.
courses.credits_text: ½ credit with encouragement to complete two semesters for one full credit
courses.prerequisites: Regenerative Agriculture / Sustainable Food Systems or instructor approval
courses.notes: Applied Capstone CRAFT Credential; Spring semester

courses.description: A C3 Internship is designed for juniors and seniors interested in gaining experience in a particular career field. Students typically spend at least two academic blocks a week “out in the field,” working with a community partner to meet established learning, workplace, and career exploration goals. Additionally, students must demonstrate proficiency in the Portrait of a Graduate competencies. C3 experiences are typically one semester, include weekly written reflection reflection and potentially career-exploration activities, and culminate with a public presentation of learning.
courses.notes: Course Requirements: Students meet with C3 staff to create a plan outlining their learning goals and; potential community partner(s). Ideally this conversation happens before the start of the semester so; that students can hit the ground running. However, if an opportunity arises later (for example, several; weeks into a new semester), C3 will work with students.; This course may count towards the CRAFT credential.; program

courses.description: A C3 Independent Study is an opportunity to explore an area of interest. Most independent studies are designed “from scratch”--students work with a C3 staff member to create a new and unique plan and identify a school or community-based mentor to support the student’s learning. Some recent examples include making art as a form of activism, starting a student investing club, and doing a science-fair project on the effect of sunscreen on coral reefs. We also offer one already-designed independent study about Holocaust survivors in Vermont, with a set of readings and activities rich in artistic expression. Additionally students must demonstrate proficiency in the Portrait of a Graduate competencies. C3 experiences are typically one semester, include frequent written reflection, and culminate with a public presentation of learning.
courses.notes: Course Requirements: Students meet with C3 staff to create a plan outlining their learning goals and; potential resources. Ideally this conversation happens before the start of the semester so that students; can hit the ground running. However, if an opportunity arises later (for example, several weeks into a; new semester), C3 will work with students.; This course may count towards the CRAFT credential.; program

courses.description: Service learning is an opportunity for students to learn new knowledge and skills while simultaneously serving the community. Students can do this work at our school or off campus. Students must demonstrate proficiency in the Portrait of a Graduate competencies. C3 experiences are typically one semester; include frequent reflection and potentially career-exploration activities; and culminate with a public presentation of learning.

Ideally this conversation happens before the start of the semester so; that students can hit the ground running. However, if an opportunity arises later (for example, several; weeks into a new semester), C3 will work with students.; This course may count towards the CRAFT credential.; program

courses.description: Teaching assistants attend all class sessions and support the classroom teacher through hands-on activities, working with small groups of students, teaching mini-lessons, preparing materials, leading discussions, and working on special projects. At the start of the semester, all TAs develop a plan that includes learning goals.. Students must demonstrate proficiency in the Portrait of a Graduate competencies. courses.description: Future You is a hands-on, semester-long course designed to support students in exploring who they are, what they value, and how they can create a meaningful future. This course invites students to reflect on their personal strengths, interests, and values while learning practical tools to navigate life’s challenges and opportunities. Using a creative and interactive approach, students will practice decision-making, build resilience, and explore diverse pathways for life after high school, whether that means college, work, or community engagement. Activities include journaling, mind-mapping, mentorship conversations, and prototyping future plans. By the end of the course, students will have developed a personal toolkit for designing their lives, including a mission statement, actionable goals, and the confidence to embrace ambiguity. Future You is about discovering your unique path and creating a fulfilling life that reflects who you are and what matters most to you.
